title: Channels, overlap, interference and transmit power

videos.script: The last lesson counted the channels in each band. This one is about living on them. {{plan}} In the 2.4 gigahertz band, channels are numbered one to thirteen. But each one is wider than the gap between two numbers, so they overlap. Only three fit side by side. One, six and eleven. {{overlap}} Two access points on the same channel take turns. That is slow, but it is orderly. Two on overlapping channels cannot understand each other, so neither one waits. Each hears the other as noise, and frames are lost. {{contention}} Part of the 5 gigahertz band belongs to radar, and a Wi-Fi network there has to move when radar appears. {{radar}} Microwave ovens, Bluetooth and baby monitors share the air too, and Wi-Fi cannot decode any of them. {{noise}} Then power. It is measured in decibels, and the arithmetic is simple once you have seen it. {{decibels}} An access point is louder than a phone. So a phone can hear it well and still not be heard back. That is why, in a busy building, turning the power down makes the network better. {{power}} Once again, the lab has no radio. What you will see here is arithmetic, and every program was run. {{no-radio}}
